newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqis blast Clinton, fear for oil deal.
newsitem.headline: Iraqis blast Clinton, fear for oil deal.

text.p: Shoppers in Baghdad cursed U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday and said Washington was reviving its vendetta against President Saddam Hussein to scupper Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.
Their concern, they said, was sparked by the use of some of the toughest remarks against the Baghdad government since U.S. President Bill Clinton took office four years ago.
Officials at the State Department on Wednesday branded the Iraqi leader a "demon" and said there were signs of a power struggle in Baghdad.

"He (Clinton) is the greatest demon. We heard the news from foreign radios. They should be ashamed of themselves to say these things," said Rasoul Baban, a Baghdadi shopper born in the Kurdish city of Sulaimaniya.
"It is clear their aim is to kill the oil deal. The U.S. delayed it when our troops liberated Arbil. Now it is using this as an excuse," said Um Salam, packing some onions and tomatoes in her basket.

When Iraqi troops sided with one Kurdish faction to drive another from the Kurdish administrative capital of Arbil in August, Washington responded by two waves of missile attacks on Iraq and a decision to delay the implementation of the Iraq-U.N. oil-for-food deal signed in May.

The deal, finally implemented in December, allows Iraq oil sales of $2 billion in six months to buy food and medicine for its more than 20 million people suffering from trade sanctions imposed by the United Nations after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990.

Iraqis have not benefited directly from the deal yet, but the flow of Iraqi crude to international markets for the first time since 1990 has lowered prices of essential goods and increased the value of the local currency against the dollar.
In Washington on Wednesday, White House spokesman Mike McCurry offered a terse but carefully worded assessment of the political situation in Baghdad.

"There are a great deal of complicated internal struggles for power" going on, McCurry said in response to questions on reports on Tuesday suggesting instability in Iraq based on comments by a senior U.S. military official.

The unnamed official said Saddam had put his wife under house arrest and was changing locations more often out of apparent fear for his safety, and that his son Uday, who was shot and wounded in Baghdad on December 12, might lose a leg to gangrene.

"Since the end of the war over Kuwait (in 1991) the U.S. has been thinking our government will fall any time and it has not. I wonder how longer they will have to wait," said a journalist who refused to be named.
An Iraqi government spokesman ridiculed the U.S. statements alleging a power struggle in Baghdad, saying they were a "distortion and propaganda ploy against Iraq".

"It seems the operating crew of information lies in Washington has resumed its tasks of misleading the public opinion in the United States and renewing fear among Kuwaiti rulers," the spokesman said in a statement published by the official Iraqi News Agency (INA) on Thursday.

Several Iraqis likened the current U.S. campaign against Iraq to the one launched when Saddam's two sons-in-law defected to Jordan in August 1995 and were killed by relatives shortly after their return to Baghdad in February 1996.
"Nothing happened in those days and nothing is going to happen now. We are all relatives and kinsmen of Saddam Hussein," said a member of the ruling Baath party.
The Baathists number more than one million. On Wednesday INA reported that two party divisions in Baghdad staged an exercise on ways of helping in the fight against crime in the country.
